questions.question: A hiker crosses Washington from west to east and notices the forests grow thinner and the land turns dry and open soon after crossing one mountain range. Which range creates that sharp climate divide?
questions.correctAnswer: The Cascade Range - its high peaks wring moisture from Pacific air, leaving eastern Washington much drier
distractors: The Olympic Mountains - they run north to south along the Canadian border
The Blue Mountains - they separate Seattle from Spokane
The Selkirk Mountains - they block all rain from reaching the coast
questions.explanation: The Cascades form a rain shadow: moist ocean air rises, cools and drops rain and snow on the western slopes, then descends dry to the east. That single fact explains the rainforests of the west and the shrub-steppe and farmland of eastern Washington.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Cascades are Washington's weather wall - wet on one side, dry on the other.

questions.question: On a map of Washington, a deep inland arm of the sea cuts between Seattle and the Olympic Peninsula, with inlets reaching down past Tacoma and Olympia. What is that waterway system called?
questions.correctAnswer: Puget Sound - a network of inlets, channels and bays carved by glaciers and connected to the Pacific Ocean
distractors: The Columbia River - a single freshwater river along the northern border
The Strait of Georgia - a lake in the center of the state
Lake Chelan - a reservoir behind Grand Coulee Dam
questions.explanation: Puget Sound was gouged out by Ice Age glaciers and is filled with salt water from the Pacific. Its ports at Seattle, Tacoma and Everett made it Washington's historic highway for trade, ferries and fishing.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Puget Sound is the sea reaching inland - Washington's front door.

questions.question: Which river forms most of Washington's southern border with Oregon before turning and cutting through the Cascades to the Pacific?
questions.correctAnswer: The Columbia River
distractors: The Snake River alone, along the entire southern border
The Willamette River
The Skagit River
questions.explanation: The Columbia begins in Canada, bends through eastern Washington, is joined by the Snake River near the Tri-Cities, then turns west to form the Oregon border. Its dams supply hydropower, irrigation water and a shipping channel.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Columbia draws Washington's southern line and lights its cities.

questions.question: A national park on Washington's northwestern peninsula protects moss-draped old-growth forest that receives around 12 feet of rain in some years. Which peninsula and forest is this?
questions.correctAnswer: The Olympic Peninsula and its temperate rainforest, including the Hoh Rainforest
distractors: The Kitsap Peninsula and its high desert
The Long Beach Peninsula and its pine barrens
The Palouse and its rainforest canopy
questions.explanation: The Olympic Mountains force ocean air upward, dumping heavy rain on their western valleys. The Hoh, Quinault and Queets valleys grow some of the largest spruce and fir trees in the world under that constant moisture.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Olympic rain grows giant trees - no umbrella survives the Hoh.

questions.question: Standing at 14,411 feet, which volcanic peak is the highest point in Washington and a landmark visible across the Puget Sound lowlands on clear days?
questions.correctAnswer: Mount Rainier
distractors: Mount Baker
Mount Adams
Mount St. Helens
questions.explanation: Mount Rainier is an active volcano and the most heavily glaciated peak in the contiguous United States. It became the fifth national park in the country in 1899 and feeds rivers such as the Nisqually and Puyallup with glacial meltwater.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Rainier rules the skyline - tallest, iciest, unforgettable.

questions.question: Farmers around Pullman grow wheat on smooth, rolling hills of deep wind-blown soil in southeastern Washington. What is this farming region called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Palouse - rolling loess hills famous for dryland wheat and lentils
distractors: The Columbia Basin - an irrigated desert plateau
The Willapa Hills - a coastal logging region
The Okanogan Highlands - a mining district
questions.explanation: Palouse soil is loess, fine dust carried by Ice Age winds and floods, piled into steep rolling hills. Growers there raise soft white wheat and lentils mostly with rainfall alone, a practice called dryland farming.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Palouse hills roll like waves - and they grow wheat, not water.

questions.question: A ferry rider leaving Seattle for Friday Harbor is traveling through an island group that once sat at the center of a border dispute. Which islands are these?
questions.correctAnswer: The San Juan Islands, between Washington and Vancouver Island
distractors: The Aleutian Islands, off Alaska
The Channel Islands, off California
The Apostle Islands, in Lake Superior
questions.explanation: The San Juans sit in the Salish Sea between the mainland and Vancouver Island. Ambiguity in the 1846 border treaty over which channel was the boundary led to the Pig War standoff of 1859, settled by arbitration in 1872.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: San Juan ferries sail through a border puzzle from 1846.

questions.question: In the 1950s, a vast irrigation project began delivering Grand Coulee Dam water - first delivered in spring 1952 - to turn dry central Washington land into orchards and fields. What is that project area called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Columbia Basin Project
distractors: The Yakima Delta Project
The Puget Lowland Project
The Spokane Aquifer Project
questions.explanation: The Columbia Basin Project pumps Columbia River water uphill from behind Grand Coulee Dam into Banks Lake, then distributes it by canals to roughly 670,000 acres. Potatoes, corn, apples and other crops now grow where sagebrush once dominated.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Grand Coulee water turned desert into dinner.

questions.question: Two large cities anchor very different regions: Seattle sits on Puget Sound in the west, but which city is the main urban center of eastern Washington, on the river that shares its name?
questions.correctAnswer: Spokane, on the Spokane River near the Idaho border
distractors: Yakima, on the Columbia River at the coast
Walla Walla, on Puget Sound
Bellingham, on the Spokane River
questions.explanation: Spokane grew around Spokane Falls, where the river's power ran mills and later generated electricity. It became the trade and rail hub of the Inland Northwest, serving eastern Washington, northern Idaho and western Montana.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Spokane is the east's anchor - built on its falls.

questions.question: A geographer divides Washington into five major land regions. A student describes lowland between the Olympics and the Cascades holding most of the state's population and biggest cities. Which region is she describing?
questions.correctAnswer: The Puget Sound Lowlands (Puget Lowland)
distractors: The Columbia Plateau
The Okanogan Highlands
The Blue Mountains region
questions.explanation: The Puget Sound Lowlands stretch from the Canadian border to the Columbia River between the Olympic and Cascade ranges. Glacial plains, the Sound's ports and a mild marine climate drew the state's largest cities, including Seattle, Tacoma and the capital, Olympia.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Most Washingtonians live in the lowland by the Sound.

questions.question: Long before statehood, Native peoples lived in Washington for thousands of years, sustained by salmon, cedar and shellfish. The phrase Washington schools use to describe that unbroken presence since the beginning is the name of the state's tribal sovereignty curriculum. What is it called?
questions.correctAnswer: Since Time Immemorial - the OSPI curriculum on tribal sovereignty in Washington State
distractors: Manifest Destiny - the OSPI curriculum on westward expansion
The Columbian Exchange - the OSPI curriculum on trade goods
New Horizons - the OSPI curriculum on space exploration
questions.explanation: Since Time Immemorial, required in Washington social studies by a 2015 law (SB 5433), teaches that tribal nations governed themselves long before the United States existed. Its units were developed with Washington's tribes and are woven into history and civics courses.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Since Time Immemorial means tribes were here first - and never left.

img.tip: STI teaches tribal sovereignty since time immemorial.

questions.question: A tribal government in Washington passes its own laws, runs its own courts and police, and manages health clinics for its citizens. A student asks where that authority comes from. Which answer is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Tribal sovereignty is inherent - Native nations governed themselves before the United States existed, and treaties and federal law recognize that self-government
distractors: Tribal authority is a gift from the Washington Legislature that it can take back at any time
Tribal governments are departments of county government
Tribal courts exist only when a governor grants permission each year
questions.explanation: Sovereignty means a nation's power to govern itself. Washington's 29 federally recognized tribes retain inherent sovereignty, limited by treaties and federal law, and deal with the United States on a government-to-government basis - not through the state.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Tribes were sovereign first - the treaties recognized it, they did not create it.

img.title: SOVEREIGN FROM THE START

questions.question: Salmon appear in the stories, ceremonies, art and diets of Native peoples across Washington, and tribal fishers still hold a First Salmon Ceremony each year. What does that ceremony honor?
questions.correctAnswer: The return of the first salmon of the season, giving thanks and ensuring the salmon people are treated with respect so they will return
distractors: The opening of a commercial cannery for the season
The anniversary of a dam's construction
The start of the tourist fishing season for visitors
questions.explanation: For Coast Salish and Plateau peoples, salmon are relatives and a sacred gift, not just food. First Salmon ceremonies, some revived after years of suppression, mark a reciprocal relationship: care for salmon and their habitat, and salmon will feed the people.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: First Salmon is gratitude in action - respect the fish, and the fish return.

img.tip: First Salmon ceremonies honor salmon's return.

questions.question: Along the coast and Puget Sound, Native families lived in large cedar-plank houses that sheltered many related families, and carved canoes from single cedar logs. Which cultural group is most associated with this way of life in western Washington?
questions.correctAnswer: The Coast Salish peoples of Puget Sound and the coast
distractors: The Plains peoples who followed bison herds
The Pueblo peoples of the desert Southwest
The Iroquois Confederacy of the Great Lakes
questions.explanation: Western red cedar gave Coast Salish peoples houses, canoes, clothing fiber and baskets - it is called the tree of life. Coast Salish carving centered on house posts and story poles; totem poles are a northern-coast form of the Haida, Tlingit and Tsimshian peoples. Village life centered on the water, where salmon, shellfish and marine mammals were harvested by family-owned fishing places.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Cedar built the Coast Salish world - houses, canoes, everything.

img.tip: Coast Salish life centered on cedar and the water.
img.title: THE CEDAR PEOPLE

questions.question: East of the Cascades, Native peoples such as the Spokane, Yakama and Colville traveled seasonally between river fisheries, root grounds and hunting areas, and lived part of the year in tule mat lodges and later tipis. Which cultural region does this describe?
questions.correctAnswer: The Plateau peoples of the Columbia Plateau in eastern Washington
distractors: The Arctic peoples of the far north coast
The Southeast peoples of the river swamps
The Great Basin peoples of the Nevada desert only
questions.explanation: Plateau life followed a seasonal round keyed to salmon runs at places like Kettle Falls and Celilo Falls, camas and bitterroot harvests, and deer hunting. The Columbia River was the region's trade highway, linking Plateau, coastal and Plains peoples.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Plateau life moved with the seasons - salmon, roots, game.

questions.question: The Makah Tribe, at the northwestern tip of the Olympic Peninsula, is famous for a traditional hunt carried out from cedar canoes and for treaties that specifically protected that right. What did the Makah traditionally hunt at sea?
questions.correctAnswer: Gray whales, along with seals and other marine mammals
distractors: Salmon only, never leaving the bay
Bison that swam to offshore islands
Polar bears on sea ice
questions.explanation: Whaling shaped Makah culture, rank and ceremony for thousands of years, a tradition confirmed by artifacts at the Ozette archaeological site. The 1855 Treaty of Neah Bay is the only United States treaty that expressly secures a tribe's whaling right.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The Makah are whalers of the cape - a right written into their treaty.

img.tip: The Makah traditionally hunted gray whales.
img.title: WHALERS OF THE CAPE

questions.question: How many federally recognized tribes have reservations or tribal lands within Washington State today?
questions.correctAnswer: 29 federally recognized tribes
distractors: 3 federally recognized tribes
12 federally recognized tribes
57 federally recognized tribes
questions.explanation: Washington's 29 federally recognized tribes include the Yakama Nation, the Confederated Tribes of the Colville Reservation, the Puyallup, Lummi, Tulalip, Muckleshoot, Nisqually and Spokane tribes, among others. Each is a separate sovereign nation with its own government and citizenship.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Twenty-nine nations within one state - remember 29.

questions.question: A tribal nation in Washington opens a natural resources department that tests river water, restores estuary habitat and co-manages salmon hatcheries with the state. Which idea best explains why the tribe does this as a government, not a charity?
questions.correctAnswer: Tribal self-governance - tribes exercise their sovereign responsibility to protect the lands, waters and treaty resources their citizens depend on
distractors: Tribes must earn permission from cities before doing environmental work
Only nonprofit groups may restore habitat in Washington
The state pays tribes to avoid doing environmental work itself
questions.explanation: Since the era of self-determination in federal Indian policy, tribes have contracted and compacted to run their own programs, from health care to fisheries science. Modern tribal governments are major employers and environmental managers across Washington.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Self-governance means tribes run their own future.

questions.question: In the late 1800s and early 1900s, many Native children in Washington were sent far from home to federal boarding schools such as the one at Chemawa in Oregon, where they were punished for speaking their languages. What was the stated federal goal of that system?
questions.correctAnswer: Forced assimilation - to erase Native languages and cultures and replace them with English and Euro-American ways
distractors: Bilingual education - to strengthen tribal languages in schools
Vocational choice - students freely picked any school they liked
Treaty fulfillment - the treaties required boarding schools
questions.explanation: Boarding schools were a tool of assimilation policy, summed up by the era's slogan about killing the Indian to save the man. Washington tribes today lead language revitalization programs, teaching Lushootseed, Ichishkiin and other Native languages to new generations.
questions.memoryHook: Boarding schools tried to erase languages - tribes are bringing them back.

img.tip: Boarding schools pursued forced assimilation.
img.title: A PAINFUL SCHOOLING ERA

questions.question: Leaders of the Puyallup Tribe and other Puget Sound tribes describe their reservations not as gifts of land from the United States, but in a different way. How do they describe them?
questions.correctAnswer: As small homelands reserved by the tribes themselves from their much larger original territories when they signed treaties
distractors: As land the tribes purchased from railroad companies
As military forts loaned to the tribes
As county parks set aside for tribal use
questions.explanation: In treaties, tribes ceded millions of acres and reserved - kept back - smaller homelands and specific rights, a principle lawyers call the reserved rights doctrine. Reservations are what tribes kept, not what the government gave.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Reservations are what tribes kept, not what they were given.

img.tip: Reservations are homelands tribes reserved.
img.title: WHAT TRIBES KEPT

questions.question: A Washington school district works directly with a nearby tribal government to design lessons about that tribe's history, rather than using only a state textbook. Which principle from the Since Time Immemorial approach does this follow?
questions.correctAnswer: Tribal history should be taught in partnership with tribes themselves, including local tribal history specific to each place
distractors: Only state officials may write any lesson about tribes
Every district must use the identical national textbook chapter
Local tribes should be mentioned only in a single heritage month
questions.explanation: OSPI built the Since Time Immemorial curriculum with tribal leaders, and state law encourages districts to collaborate with neighboring tribes. A lesson about the Snoqualmie Tribe near the Cascades foothills should differ from one about the Makah at Neah Bay, because each nation's history is its own.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Local tribal history, taught with the tribe - that is the STI way.

img.tip: STI lessons are built in partnership with tribes.

questions.question: Before contact with Europeans, trade networks moved dentalium shells from the coast, obsidian from volcanic areas and dried salmon far inland across the region that is now Washington. What does the scale of that trade show about Native societies here?
questions.correctAnswer: They were organized, prosperous societies with governments, property systems and long-distance commerce long before Europeans arrived
distractors: They had no economies until fur traders arrived
They lived completely isolated from one another
They relied entirely on Europeans for tools and food
questions.explanation: Archaeology and tribal oral histories document ranked villages, family-owned resource sites, potlatch redistribution ceremonies and trade reaching hundreds of miles. The fur trade later plugged into Native trade networks that already existed - it did not create them.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Trade here is ancient - Europeans joined a system already running.

img.tip: Native trade networks were ancient and extensive.

questions.question: In December 1854, Territorial Governor Isaac Stevens met Nisqually and Puyallup leaders at a council on a creek near the Nisqually Delta. The treaty signed there was the first of the Stevens treaties in Washington. Which treaty was it?
questions.correctAnswer: The Treaty of Medicine Creek (1854)
distractors: The Treaty of Point Elliott (1855)
The Treaty of Walla Walla (1855)
The Treaty of Neah Bay (1855)
questions.explanation: At Medicine Creek, the Nisqually, Puyallup and Squaxin Island tribes ceded about 2.24 million acres and reserved small reservations. Its fishing language - the right to fish at usual and accustomed grounds in common with settlers - later became central to the Boldt decision.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Medicine Creek was first - December 1854.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a winter council gathering under tall fir trees near a creek, tribal leaders and territorial officials seated facing each other, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Medicine Creek (1854) was the first Stevens treaty.
img.title: THE FIRST TREATY

questions.question: Almost every Stevens treaty in Washington contains nearly identical words protecting the right of taking fish at usual and accustomed grounds and stations. Why do those words matter so much today?
questions.correctAnswer: They reserved tribal fishing rights in the treaties themselves, so the rights survived statehood and were later upheld in federal court
distractors: They were a polite greeting with no legal meaning
They gave all fishing rights in Washington to the territory
They expired automatically when Washington became a state in 1889
questions.explanation: Treaties are the supreme law of the land under the US Constitution, and courts read them as the tribes would have understood them. The reserved fishing right became the legal foundation for tribal fisheries, the fish wars protests and Judge Boldt's 1974 ruling.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Usual and accustomed - three words that still feed families.

No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Treaty language reserved tribal fishing rights.
img.title: USUAL AND ACCUSTOMED

questions.question: In January 1855, leaders of the Duwamish, Suquamish and other Puget Sound peoples signed a treaty at Mukilteo that ceded the land where Seattle now stands. Chief Seattle and Chief Patkanim were among the signers. Which treaty was this?
questions.correctAnswer: The Treaty of Point Elliott (1855)
distractors: The Treaty of Medicine Creek (1854)
The Treaty of Point No Point (1855)
The Yakima Treaty (1855)
questions.explanation: Point Elliott created reservations including Tulalip, Swinomish, Lummi and Port Madison, and reserved fishing and hunting rights. The city of Seattle takes its name from Si'ahl, the Duwamish and Suquamish leader who signed for his peoples.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Point Elliott gave Seattle its land story - and its name.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of a council on a Puget Sound beach in winter with canoes drawn up and leaders gathered around a fire, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. img.tip: Point Elliott (1855) covered the Seattle area.
img.title: THE SEATTLE-AREA TREATY

questions.question: Governor Isaac Stevens pushed Washington's treaties through in little more than a year, using interpreters and a trade jargon called Chinook Jargon that had only a few hundred words. Why do historians and courts treat that fact as important?
questions.correctAnswer: Complex legal ideas like land cession were explained through a limited trade language, so treaties must be interpreted as the tribes understood them, with ambiguities resolved in the tribes' favor
distractors: It proves the treaties were written perfectly clearly
It means the treaties were never signed at all
It shows Stevens spoke every Native language fluently
questions.explanation: Chinook Jargon lacked words for concepts like fee-simple ownership, and many Native signers could not read English. Federal courts therefore apply canons of treaty interpretation: understand the treaty as the tribal signers did, and resolve unclear terms in favor of the tribes.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A few hundred jargon words carried away millions of acres - courts remember that.

img.scene: Mature educational illustration of an interpreter speaking between two seated groups at a treaty council, with documents on a blanket between them, with a small matured green-to-purple gradient dinosaur guide with orange eyes and white fangs standing calmly nearby. No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.
img.tip: Treaties are read as tribes understood them.
img.title: WORDS THAT FELL SHORT

questions.question: Anger over the Stevens treaties, shrinking reservations and miners rushing onto Yakama land helped spark armed conflict in 1855 to 1858 across the territory. What is that conflict generally called?
questions.correctAnswer: The Puget Sound and Yakima wars - including the Yakima War in the east and fighting around Puget Sound in the west
distractors: The Pig War, fought entirely over a single pig
The Nez Perce War of 1877 only, with no earlier fighting
The War of 1812 in the Pacific Northwest
questions.explanation: Leschi, a Nisqually leader who had resisted the Medicine Creek Treaty's tiny reservation, became a central figure and was hanged in 1858 after a controversial trial; a Historical Court of Inquiry exonerated him in 2004, in a symbolic ruling with no legal significance. Kamiakin led Yakama resistance in the east until the fighting ended in 1858.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Broken treaty promises lit the wars of 1855 to 1858.

No readable text, no words, no letters, no numbers anywhere in the image.

questions.question: In the 1960s and early 1970s, tribal members including Nisqually activist Billy Frank Jr. held fish-ins on the Puyallup and Nisqually rivers, deliberately fishing in defiance of state rules to assert treaty rights. What were they protesting and claiming?

distractors: That salmon should never be eaten by anyone
That the federal government should close all rivers to fishing
That tribes wanted to fish only in other states
questions.explanation: State officials blamed tribal nets for declining salmon runs while allowing large commercial and sport harvests, and tribal fishers took only a small share of the catch. questions.question: In 1974, Federal Judge George H. Boldt ruled in United States v. Washington after a long trial in Tacoma. What was the core of his decision, known everywhere as the Boldt decision?
questions.correctAnswer: Treaty tribes reserved the right to take up to 50 percent of the harvestable salmon at their usual and accustomed grounds, and tribes became co-managers of the fishery with the state
distractors: Tribes could take 5 percent of the salmon as a welfare benefit
All commercial fishing in Washington must end permanently
The treaties had expired and tribes had no fishing rights at all
questions.explanation: Boldt read the treaty phrase 'in common with' to mean tribes could take up to half the harvestable fish passing their grounds. The US Supreme Court largely upheld the ruling in 1979, and the decision transformed tribes into co-managers of Washington salmon.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Boldt: in common with means up to half.

questions.question: After the Boldt decision, how is salmon management in Washington actually carried out each year?
questions.correctAnswer: The state and the treaty tribes act as co-managers, jointly setting seasons, harvest levels and hatchery plans to protect the runs
distractors: The state manages alone and informs tribes afterward
A private company sets all fishing rules
Only the federal government sets seasons, with no state role
questions.explanation: Co-management grew from conflict into an institution: tribal and state scientists jointly model runs, negotiate annual agreements such as the Puget Sound harvest plan, and work on habitat. Judge Boldt retained court jurisdiction, and later phases of the case covered shellfish and habitat culverts.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: From court fight to co-management - that is Boldt's legacy at work.

questions.correctAnswer: The Supreme Court upheld the heart of the ruling, confirming the tribes' right to up to 50 percent of harvestable fish

The Supreme Court refused to hear any part of the case
The Supreme Court ruled treaties apply only in Oregon
questions.explanation: In Washington v. Washington State Commercial Passenger Fishing Vessel Association (1979), the Supreme Court affirmed the treaty interpretation, with modest adjustments. The decision stands as one of the most important affirmations of treaty rights in American law.

All highways in Washington were ordered closed
The Boldt decision itself was overturned

It founded the city of Seattle
It proved Washington was an island
questions.explanation: Gray's entry into the Columbia, building on his earlier coastal trade, let the United States argue it had discovered and explored the river. Explorers Lewis and Clark, Britain's David Thompson and Gray's voyage all became evidence in the Oregon boundary dispute.

Puget was a Native word Vancouver recorded for the whole sea
questions.explanation: Lieutenant Peter Puget led boat parties into the deep southern inlets below the Tacoma Narrows in May 1792. Vancouver applied Puget's name to those southern waters, and usage later extended it to the whole sound system.

It built the first railroad to the Pacific
It signed the treaties that created Washington Territory
questions.explanation: Sent by President Thomas Jefferson and guided in part by Sacagawea, the Corps of Discovery wintered at Fort Clatsop on the Oregon side in 1805-1806. questions.question: In 1825, the Hudson's Bay Company built a fort on the north bank of the Columbia that became the fur trade capital of the region, with farms, mills and a diverse workforce. Which fort was it, and who led it for two decades?
questions.correctAnswer: Fort Vancouver, led by Chief Factor John McLoughlin
distractors: Fort Spokane, led by Captain George Vancouver
Fort Nisqually, led by Governor Isaac Stevens
Fort Walla Walla, led by Marcus Whitman only
questions.explanation: John McLoughlin, called the Father of Oregon, ran Fort Vancouver as a self-sufficient depot that supplied brigades across the Northwest. He famously aided exhausted American settlers arriving on the Oregon Trail, even though his company served British interests.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Fort Vancouver was the fur era's capital - McLoughlin its mayor in all but name.

questions.question: Sea otter pelts from the Northwest Coast sold for high prices in China, drawing American and British ships in the maritime fur trade. What did that trade do to Native coastal societies and to the otters?
questions.correctAnswer: It enriched some Native trading chiefs and spread new goods - and firearms and disease - while sea otters were hunted nearly to extinction
distractors: It left Native societies completely unchanged
It increased sea otter numbers across the coast
It ended all trade between Native groups
questions.explanation: Ship captains traded metal goods and guns for pelts that Native hunters supplied through their own trade systems. By the early 1800s sea otters were commercially wiped out in many areas; they were protected much later and reintroduced to the Washington coast in 1969-1970.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A pelt worth a fortune in China nearly erased the otter.

questions.question: In 1811, John Jacob Astor's men founded the first American fur post at the mouth of the Columbia, a settlement later sold to a British company during the War of 1812. Which post was it?
questions.correctAnswer: Fort Astoria (Fort George under the British)
distractors: Fort Vancouver, founded in 1825
Fort Colville, founded for mining
Fort Steilacoom, founded by the Army
questions.explanation: Astoria, in present-day Oregon just across the river from Washington, anchored the Pacific Fur Company's attempt to link Columbia furs to China. Its sale to the North West Company in 1813 shows how the War of 1812 reached even the remote Northwest Coast.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Astoria was America's first foothold at the river's mouth.

questions.question: Fur brigades carried beaver pelts and supplies on a famous trail from Fort Vancouver eastward through the Columbia Gorge and north into the interior. What sustained the fur trade at posts like Spokane House and Fort Colville?
questions.correctAnswer: Native trappers, traders and guides whose knowledge, labor and trade networks made the posts work
distractors: Steam locomotives delivering furs year round
Gold miners working in winter camps
Only British soldiers stationed at each post
questions.explanation: Posts depended on Native peoples as trappers, provisioners, interpreters and family partners, and on French-Canadian and Hawaiian (Kanaka) workers. Spokane House (1810) and Fort Colville (1825) traded within Indigenous economies that predated them by centuries.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: No Native knowledge, no fur trade - the posts ran on it.

questions.question: Long before explorers arrived, a Spanish claim rested on a 1592 tale of a Greek pilot sailing a great strait at about Washington's latitude. The waterway between Vancouver Island and the mainland now carries his name. Who was he said to be, and what is the strait called?
questions.correctAnswer: Juan de Fuca - the Strait of Juan de Fuca
distractors: Juan Cabrillo - the Strait of Cabrillo
Ferdinand Magellan - the Strait of Anian only
Sebastian Vizcaino - the Strait of Georgia
questions.explanation: The mariner known as Juan de Fuca (born Ioannis Fokas) claimed to have found the fabled Strait of Anian for Spain. No proof of his voyage survives, but British captain Charles Barkley applied the name in 1787 to the real strait, which forms part of the US-Canada border today.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: A possibly tall tale still labels the map: Juan de Fuca.

questions.question: From 1818 to 1846, the United States and Britain agreed to jointly occupy the Oregon Country rather than fight over it. How was that long dispute finally settled?
questions.correctAnswer: The Oregon Treaty of 1846 set the boundary at the 49th parallel west to the sea, with Vancouver Island remaining British
distractors: The Treaty of Medicine Creek gave all of it to the United States
A popular vote of settlers gave all of it to Britain
The Pig War ended with Britain keeping the mainland
questions.explanation: The treaty extended the familiar 49th parallel line through the Rockies to the coast, dipping around Vancouver Island. Vague wording about the water boundary near the San Juan Islands left one dispute behind, settled peacefully in 1872.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1846: the 49th parallel became Washington's northern edge.

questions.question: Thousands of American families traveled the Oregon Trail in the 1840s, many settling first in the Willamette Valley, then spreading north of the Columbia. What federal law of 1850 fueled settlement by granting land to white settlers?
questions.correctAnswer: The Donation Land Claim Act - it gave large claims to settlers who arrived and farmed the land, on territory taken from Native peoples
distractors: The Homestead Act of 1862, applied retroactively to 1830
The Indian Removal Act, which granted land only to tribes
The Land Ordinance of 1785, written for Washington
questions.explanation: The Act promised 320 acres to a single settler and 640 to a married couple who arrived before December 1850 and cultivated for four years. It recognized and extinguished Native title on paper before treaties were negotiated north of the Columbia, accelerating dispossession.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Free land for settlers meant taken land for tribes - both halves are the story.

questions.question: In 1836, Marcus and Narcissa Whitman founded a mission among the Cayuse people near present-day Walla Walla. What did the Whitmans do there besides preach?
questions.correctAnswer: They ran a way station for Oregon Trail emigrants, farmed with irrigation, and provided medical care - while bringing diseases and cultural pressure that strained relations with the Cayuse
distractors: They operated a gold mine and a bank
They commanded an army fort on the Columbia
They printed Washington's first state constitution
questions.explanation: Whitman Mission became a major stop where wagon trains rested and resupplied. Measles carried by emigrants devastated the Cayuse, who had little immunity, while settler numbers kept rising on Cayuse land - tensions that ended in violence in 1847.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: The mission was a crossroads - of help, disease and conflict.

questions.question: In November 1847, Cayuse men attacked the Whitman mission and killed Marcus and Narcissa Whitman and 11 others. What was the attack's immediate background?
questions.correctAnswer: A measles epidemic was killing many Cayuse while most white patients recovered, and Cayuse grievances over disease, land and the mission's role had deepened
distractors: A dispute over the price of wheat alone
The Cayuse were ordered to attack by British officials
A gold discovery on mission land that same week
questions.explanation: Whitman treated both peoples as a doctor, but measles mortality fell overwhelmingly on the Cayuse. The killings triggered the Cayuse War and pushed Congress to organize Oregon Territory in 1848, reshaping federal control of the region.

Moving Oregon's capital to Seattle
Annexing the area to Canada until statehood

questions.question: In 1859, an American farmer on San Juan Island shot a British company's pig rooting in his potato patch, and both nations sent warships and troops. How did the Pig War end?
questions.correctAnswer: With no battle at all - joint military occupation lasted until 1872, when an arbitrator awarded the islands to the United States

With Britain annexing all of Puget Sound
With the farmer becoming governor of the island

Olympia - named for Mount Olympus in Greece only
Everett - named for its founder's ship

The Union Pacific - Tacoma was billed as the Rose City
The Southern Pacific - Tacoma was billed as the Inland Empire

The 42nd state - first governor George Turner
The 50th state - first governor John Rankin Rogers

questions.question: Delegates writing the Washington Constitution in 1889 produced a document much longer and more detailed than the US Constitution. Why?
questions.correctAnswer: They distrusted legislatures and corporations after territorial scandals, so they wrote detailed limits and rules directly into the constitution
distractors: They were paid by the word and stretched the text
They copied the British constitution word for word
The US Constitution was banned as a model
questions.explanation: Progressive-era suspicion of railroads and graft shaped the 1889 convention in Olympia. The result regulates everything from public lands and water to corporate power, and it still contains the original articles alongside more than 100 amendments.

questions.question: Article IX of the Washington Constitution says it is the paramount duty of the state to make ample provision for the education of all children living within its borders. What has that sentence done in modern times?
questions.correctAnswer: It became the basis of court rulings, including the McCleary decision, holding that the state must fully fund basic education before other programs
distractors: It was repealed in 1900 and has no effect today
It applies only to private schools
It sets the price of college tuition each year
questions.explanation: Paramount means first and highest - stronger education language than in most state constitutions. In McCleary v. questions.correctAnswer: The initiative - adopted by constitutional amendment in 1912, along with the referendum
distractors: The filibuster - adopted in 1889 at statehood
The recall alone - adopted in 1950
The pocket veto - adopted in 1912 for citizens
questions.explanation: Washington was an early direct-democracy state: initiative and referendum came in 1912 and the recall of elected officials in 1911. The first successful initiative, in 1914, prohibited alcohol statewide - five years before national Prohibition.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 1912 gave voters a pen of their own: the initiative.

questions.correctAnswer: Washington Territory had briefly given women the vote in the 1880s before courts struck it down, so suffragists fought for a permanent constitutional amendment in 1910

The 1910 vote applied only to school board elections
Congress ordered Washington to adopt women's suffrage in 1910
questions.explanation: Territorial women voted in 1883-1887 until territorial supreme court decisions ended the experiment. The 1910 amendment, won by organizers like Emma Smith DeVoe, made Washington a suffrage leader and helped build momentum for the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Washington women won the vote, lost it, then won it for good in 1910.

questions.question: The Washington Constitution's Declaration of Rights (Article I) protects freedoms such as speech, religion and jury trial. How does it sometimes protect Washingtonians more than the US Bill of Rights does?
questions.correctAnswer: State courts can read Washington's own rights provisions more broadly than the federal floor, giving extra protection under state law
distractors: Article I replaced the US Bill of Rights entirely in Washington
Article I applies only to state employees
State rights can never exceed federal rights in any state

The rush bankrupted Seattle within a year
Gold was discovered inside Seattle city limits

questions.question: Frederick Weyerhaeuser's 1900 purchase of 900,000 acres of Washington timberland from the Northern Pacific, at about six dollars an acre, is often called the largest private land deal of its time. What industry did it anchor?
questions.correctAnswer: The industrial timber industry - corporate logging, sawmills and later tree farming that made Washington a top lumber state
distractors: The whaling industry of the outer coast
The wheat export trade of the Palouse
The aircraft industry of the Puget Sound region
questions.explanation: Weyerhaeuser's purchase began the shift from independent gyppo loggers to vast corporate tree farms. Timber built towns like Aberdeen, Everett (the world's lumber capital in its boom) and Longview, and timber taxes and jobs dominated western Washington for generations.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: 900,000 acres at six dollars each changed Washington forests forever.

questions.question: Fallers with crosscut saws (nicknamed misery whips), steam donkey engines and logging railroads took down Douglas-fir trees centuries old. What eventually forced the timber industry to change in the late 1900s?
questions.correctAnswer: Old-growth depletion, mechanization, market shifts and environmental protection - especially the northern spotted owl listing (1990) and the Northwest Forest Plan (1994)

The invention of plastic replacing all wood use
Earthquakes destroying every sawmill at once

questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Owls, automation and empty hillsides ended the old timber boom.

questions.question: The Yakima Valley today produces most of the nation's hops and huge shares of its apples, cherries and wine grapes. What made that desert valley bloom?

distractors: Natural rainfall averaging 40 inches a year
Glacier water piped from Mount Rainier by gravity alone
Underground lakes discovered under every farm in 1950
questions.explanation: With only about eight inches of rain a year, the valley depends on stored snowmelt and canals. Washington is the nation's top apple state, and its orchards and vineyards in the Columbia and Yakima valleys supply most US hops and a major wine industry.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Eight inches of rain, first in apples - the difference is irrigation.

questions.question: Washington wheat country tells two different stories: Palouse growers farm with rainfall alone, while Columbia Basin growers use irrigation. What is the Palouse method called, and why does it work there?
questions.correctAnswer: Dryland farming - it works because deep loess soil stores winter moisture that carries wheat through the dry summer

Aquaponics - wheat grows in fish tanks
Terrace farming on mountain slopes above the clouds
questions.explanation: Palouse farmers summer-fallow some fields - resting them a year to bank moisture - and breed wheat varieties for low rainfall. The region's steep hills required special hillside combines that level themselves on slopes up to about 45 percent.
questions.memoryHook: T-Rexy says: Banking winter water in deep soil: that is dryland farming.

They were annexed by Canada under the mill treaties
They switched instantly to aircraft manufacturing

It shows Washington never relied on natural resources
It shows salmon were imported from the Atlantic for canning

The Peace Corps, founded in 1961

questions.question: In 1943, the federal government secretly built a small city at Hanford in the Columbia Basin desert to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project, displacing farmers and the Wanapum people. What is Hanford's legacy today?

It was abandoned in 1945 with no contamination
It now produces electricity at the B Reactor for the grid

questions.question: After Pearl Harbor, President Franklin Roosevelt's Executive Order 9066 led to the forced removal of more than 12,000 Japanese Americans from western Washington. Where were many Puget Sound families first held, close to home?
questions.correctAnswer: At the Puyallup fairgrounds, renamed Camp Harmony - a temporary assembly center surrounded by barbed wire before transfer to camps like Minidoka in Idaho

At their own farms under a curfew only, never removed
At a resort on Bainbridge Island built for evacuees

questions.question: A Black shipyard worker arriving in Seattle or Vancouver, Washington in 1943 found booming wages - and segregated housing and union barriers. Which wartime change began opening those doors?

The shipyards' decision to hire only local residents
A court ruling that ended all discrimination in 1942

questions.question: Salmon runs that once filled Washington rivers have fallen so far that many are listed under the Endangered Species Act, and orca whales that eat Chinook salmon are endangered too. Which combination do scientists and tribal and state governments identify as the core problems?

A single invasive fish that ate all the salmon in 1990
Overprotection of forests along every river in the state
